doc.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012

title: Accompanying vocalists: challenging singers and less is more
summary: He prefers working with better singers, avoids playing the melody, uses silence, and learned this accompanying a college vocal group.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Who’s the more challenging vocalist to work with usually, the fabulous vocalist or the vocalist who maybe shouldn’t be doing this gig.

Keep your daughter off the stage Mrs. Worthington? The latter. Because you always want to work with people who are better than you, people who can do something that you can’t do. Because then you’re learning. Because otherwise if you’re just picking somebody up, you’re spending all your time babysitting and you’re not learning.
Yeah. You probably get a sense fairly quickly in working with a particular singer like I need to lead this person a little bit or not be too — my substitutions, watch out for them. Right.

Um hum. Well I look to people like Nelson Riddle, Axle Stordahl and even people with film scores like Erich Korngold, you just listen to what’s going on behind the action. And you know how much you can get away with almost immediately if you’re doing stuff and they get lost. But that rarely happens. I mean usually they can follow. Because they’re used to playing with something — in other words I will stray from the standard changes after a chorus or two. And the vocalists welcome that. They actually are happy that I’m doing that instead of just playing some basic cotton candy arrangement that’s written bare bones for somebody to play with their hands about this far apart. And they’re about this far apart and it actually sounds a little bit more orchestral for some reason. More jazzy. And people, I find that vocalists do enjoy that, and I never play the melody. I remember learning that a long time ago. I played for a vocal jazz group in college. A professor named Robert Porter, a great professor out at the University of Wisconsin Milwaukee. I © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

audited the class. I did it because I just wanted to meet girls. But I was playing with them and I learned, again, less is more, don’t try to overplay them, don’t try to upstage them. Just do your thing. If they look good you look good. And again, a lot of times I’ll actually take my hands completely off the keys and I’ll allow some silence. Because if there’s a vocal person, that’s a brave thing to do. I know that as a heavy metal singer too. Getting up and singing in front of a crowd is a brave thing to do. You know if a vocalist is doing it and somebody is yapping away in the audience, one way to make them knock it off is to have these moments of silence where you can hear a pin drop. And they’ll stop talking. It happens. It’s a powerful thing and it makes everybody feel better because they think how cool are we as an audience to have just done that. And it’s like crack, you immediately are seduced into craving more, I want that, I want that silent moment again. So yeah, silence is golden when you’re accompanying a vocalist.
